    3.1 Checking input

    The code for this section is in 3.1_code/checking_input.py.

    Why check input?

    Programs receive data from outside: a person typing, a file, a web form. That data can be wrong. Someone types their age as abc. A file has an empty cell. A form field holds 5,000 characters where you expected 10.

    Validation means checking data before you use it. A program that validates its input gives a clear message instead of crashing. It also keeps bad values out of your data, where they would spoil every later result.

    Validation matters for security too. Many security problems start with a program that trusted its input. A good habit is to treat all outside data as unchecked until your code has checked it.

    Five kinds of check

    Check Question it asks Example
    Presence Is there a value at all? A username must not be empty.
    Type Is it the right kind of value? An age must be a whole number.
    Range Is the number between the limits? An age must be from 0 to 120.
    Length Does it have the right number of characters? A postcode has exactly 4 characters.
    Allowed characters Does it use only the characters we accept? A username uses only letters, digits and _.

    The rest of this section shows each check in Python.

    Presence: is anything there?

    input() always returns a string. If the person presses Enter straight away, it returns the empty string "". A string of only spaces is also no real answer. Use strip() (Week 1) to remove spaces from both ends first.

    PYTHON 

    name = "   "
if name.strip() == "":
    print("Please type a name.")

    OUTPUT 

    Please type a name.

    Type: is it the right kind of value?

    There are two ways to check that a string holds a whole number.

    Way 1: isdigit(). This string method returns True when every character is a digit and there is at least one character.

    PYTHON 

    print("42".isdigit())
print("4 2".isdigit())
print("-5".isdigit())
print("".isdigit())

    OUTPUT 

    True
False
False
False

    Notice that "-5" gives False, because - is not a digit. So isdigit() suits values that are made only of digits, such as a postcode.

    Way 2: try / except ValueError. You met this in Part 1. Try to convert the string with int(). If Python raises a ValueError, the string was not a whole number.

    PYTHON 

    def is_valid_age(text):
    """Return True if text is a whole number from 0 to 120."""
    try:
        age = int(text)
    except ValueError:
        return False
    return 0 <= age <= 120

    This way accepts "-5" as a number, and it also accepts spaces around the number, because int(" 61 ") is 61. The last line of the function is the next check.

    Range and length

    A range check asks whether a number is between two limits. Python lets you write both limits in one line: 0 <= age <= 120.

    PYTHON 

    for text in ["34", "abc", "-5", "150", " 61 "]:
    print(repr(text), is_valid_age(text))

    OUTPUT 

    '34' True
'abc' False
'-5' False
'150' False
' 61 ' True

    repr(text) shows the string with its quotation marks, so you can see the spaces.

    A length check uses len(). An Australian postcode is exactly four digits, so it needs a length check and a type check together.

    PYTHON 

    def is_valid_postcode(text):
    """Return True if text is exactly four digits, such as "6000"."""
    return len(text) == 4 and text.isdigit()


for text in ["6000", "0800", "600", "60000", "6OOO"]:
    print(repr(text), is_valid_postcode(text))

    OUTPUT 

    '6000' True
'0800' True
'600' False
'60000' False
'6OOO' False

    The last one uses the capital letter O, not zero. It looks right to a person, but the check catches it.

    Keep a postcode as a string. Do not convert it with int(). The postcode "0800" would become the number 800, and the leading zero would be lost.

    any and all

    Some checks ask a question about every character in a string. Python has two built-in functions for this. Both take a list of True and False values.

    • any(...) returns True if at least one value is True.
    • all(...) returns True if every value is True.

    PYTHON 

    print(any([False, True, False]))
print(all([True, True, False]))

    OUTPUT 

    True
False

    You can build the list with a list comprehension (Part 1, Week 4). This asks “is at least one character a digit?”:

    PYTHON 

    print(any([ch.isdigit() for ch in "kettle7"]))

    OUTPUT 

    True

    When the comprehension is the only thing inside the brackets of any or all, you may leave out the square brackets. It works the same way and is easier to read.

    PYTHON 

    print(any(ch.isdigit() for ch in "kettle7"))
print(all(ch.isdigit() for ch in "60o0"))

    OUTPUT 

    True
False

    Read the first line aloud as “any character is a digit, for each character in the text”. The string methods isupper(), islower(), isdigit() and isalpha() (is it a letter?) all work on a single character in this way.

    To test for symbols, there is no ready-made method. Make a set of the symbols you mean, and use in.

    PYTHON 

    SYMBOLS = set("!@#$%&*?")


def has_symbol(text):
    """Return True if at least one character is in SYMBOLS."""
    return any(ch in SYMBOLS for ch in text)


print(has_symbol("kettle!"))
print(has_symbol("kettle"))

    OUTPUT 

    True
False

    set("!@#$%&*?") makes a set with one item for each character in the string.

    Allowed characters: allow-list and block-list

    There are two ways to decide which characters are acceptable.

    • An allow-list names everything you accept. Anything else is refused.
    • A block-list names everything you refuse. Anything else is accepted.

    An allow-list is safer. With a block-list you must think of every bad character in advance, and you will miss some. With an allow-list, a character you never thought about is refused automatically.

    PYTHON 

    ALLOWED = set("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789_")

name = "olivia_t"
print(all(ch in ALLOWED for ch in name))

name = "olivia t;"
print(all(ch in ALLOWED for ch in name))

    OUTPUT 

    True
False

    The second name has a space and a semicolon. Neither is in the allow-list, so the name is refused. Nobody had to list the space or the semicolon as “bad”.

    Returning a list of problems

    A function that returns only True or False cannot tell the user what to fix. A function that stops at the first problem makes the user fix one thing, try again, and then meet the next problem.

    A friendlier pattern is to collect every problem in a list and return the list. An empty list means the value is fine.

    PYTHON 

    def check_username(name):
    """Return a list of problems with a username. Empty means it is fine."""
    problems = []
    if name.strip() == "":
        problems.append("The username is empty.")
        return problems
    if len(name) < 3:
        problems.append("The username is shorter than 3 characters.")
    if len(name) > 15:
        problems.append("The username is longer than 15 characters.")
    if not all(ch in ALLOWED for ch in name):
        problems.append("Use only lower-case letters, digits and underscores.")
    if name[0].isdigit():
        problems.append("The username must not start with a digit.")
    return problems


for name in ["olivia_t", "", "jw", "9 Lives!", "user01"]:
    print(repr(name), check_username(name))

    OUTPUT 

    'olivia_t' []
'' ['The username is empty.']
'jw' ['The username is shorter than 3 characters.']
'9 Lives!' ['Use only lower-case letters, digits and underscores.', 'The username must not start with a digit.']
'user01' []

    Three things to notice:

    1. Each check is a separate if, not elif. With elif, Python would stop at the first problem.
    2. The empty name returns early. The other checks make no sense on an empty name, and name[0] would raise an IndexError.
    3. The function is pure: it takes a value and returns a value. It does not call input() or print(). That makes it easy to test, and you will use the same pattern in this week’s Build.

    Common mistakes

    • Using elif when you want every problem. Use a separate if for each check.
    • Trusting all on an empty string. all(ch.isdigit() for ch in "") is True, because there is no character that fails. Check presence or length first.
    • Using isdigit() for numbers that may be negative or have a decimal point. "-5".isdigit() and "3.5".isdigit() are both False. Use try / except ValueError with int() or float().
    • Converting codes to numbers. Postcodes and phone numbers are text. int("0800") loses the zero.
    • Writing a block-list. Refusing a few known bad characters lets through everything you forgot. List what you accept.
    • Checking after using. Validate first, then use the value.
    Challenge

    Exercises: Level 1

    1. Write is_present(text). It returns True if the text has at least one character that is not a space. Test it with "", " " and "Jack".

    2. Write is_valid_year(text). It returns True if the text is a whole number from 1900 to 2026. Use try / except ValueError. Test it with "1987", "87", "abc" and "2050".

    3. Write is_valid_state(text). It returns True if the text, in upper case, is in the set {"WA", "NT", "SA", "QLD", "NSW", "VIC", "TAS", "ACT"}. Is this an allow-list or a block-list? Write your answer in a comment.

    4. Without running it, predict what each line prints. Then run it to check.

      PYTHON 

      print(any(ch.isupper() for ch in "kettle7"))
print(all(ch.islower() for ch in "kettle7"))
print(all(ch.isalpha() for ch in "kettle"))

    5. Write check_pin(text). It returns a list of problems. A PIN must be exactly 4 characters, must be all digits, and must not be "0000" or "1234". Test it with "4821", "12a" and "1234".

    Challenge

    Exercises: Level 2

    1. Add a check to check_username that the name does not end with an underscore. Test it.
    2. Write check_phone(text) for an Australian mobile number written as ten digits that start with 04. First remove any spaces with replace(" ", ""). Return a list of problems. Use made-up numbers only.

    3.2 Hashing with hashlib

    The code for this section is in 3.2_code/hashing.py.

    Why hashing matters

    You download a large file. How do you know it arrived complete, and that nobody changed it on the way? You keep a report for a year. How can you show it is the same report today?

    Comparing two large files byte by byte is slow, and you may not have the original. Instead, you compare two short fingerprints. This is called checking integrity: checking that data has not changed.

    What a hash is

    A hash function takes any data and calculates a short, fixed-length value from it. That value is called a hash or a digest. Think of it as a fingerprint of the data.

    This course uses a hash function called SHA-256. It is a widely used standard. Its digest is always 256 bits long. Written in hexadecimal (digits 0 to 9 and letters a to f), that is always 64 characters.

    Python’s built-in module hashlib provides SHA-256. Nothing needs to be installed.

    Hashing text

    PYTHON 

    import hashlib

text = "hello"
digest = hashlib.sha256(text.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
print(digest)
print(len(digest))

    OUTPUT 

    2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824
64

    Read the long line from the inside out:

    1. text.encode("utf-8") turns the string into bytes. A hash function works on bytes, not on characters. In Week 1 you saw that encode turns text into the numbers that are really stored. If you forget it, Python raises a TypeError.
    2. hashlib.sha256(...) calculates the hash of those bytes.
    3. .hexdigest() gives the result as a string of 64 hexadecimal characters.

    You will hash text often, so wrap the line in a function:

    PYTHON 

    def text_hash(text):
    """Return the SHA-256 hash of a string, as 64 hexadecimal characters."""
    return hashlib.sha256(text.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

    Three properties to remember

    1. The same input always gives the same hash. It does not matter which computer, which day, or which program.

    PYTHON 

    print(text_hash("hello") == text_hash("hello"))

    OUTPUT 

    True

    2. A tiny change gives a very different hash. These two messages differ in one character.

    PYTHON 

    print(text_hash("Pay Jack $100"))
print(text_hash("Pay Jack $900"))

    OUTPUT 

    b9d6c4b2010b10a0d377302124d9fa036c33280d4ce74e1d67ee1fb29e5c108e
c55c9148b69a949a626999d3cbbcedc46fce25a55c0f0a125b2e8d9ec6a1f2ef

    The two digests have nothing visible in common. So a hash shows that data changed. It does not show what changed or how much.

    3. It is one-way. You cannot work back from the hash to the data. There is no “unhash” function. The digest is 64 characters whether the input is one letter or a whole book, so the data is simply not in there.

    PYTHON 

    print(len(text_hash("a")))
print(len(text_hash("a" * 100000)))

    OUTPUT 

    64
64

    Hashing is also exact. "Hello" and "hello" have different hashes. So do "hello" and "hello " with a space at the end.

    Hashing a file

    Until now you have opened files in text mode, where Python decodes the bytes into characters for you. For a hash you want the exact bytes on the disk. Open the file in binary mode by adding "b" to the mode: "rb" means “read, binary”. In binary mode read() returns a bytes value, not a string, and you do not give an encoding.

    PYTHON 

    def file_hash(path):
    """Return the SHA-256 hash of a file, read in binary mode."""
    with open(path, "rb") as file:
        data = file.read()
    return hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()

    There is no encode this time, because data is already bytes.

    To try it, the next lines save a small file that holds the five bytes of hello, then hash it. "wb" means “write, binary”.

    PYTHON 

    from pathlib import Path

demo = Path(__file__).with_name("demo_note.txt")
with open(demo, "wb") as file:
    file.write("hello".encode("utf-8"))

print(file_hash(demo))
print(file_hash(demo) == text_hash("hello"))

    OUTPUT 

    2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824
True

    Path(__file__).with_name("demo_note.txt") means “a file called demo_note.txt in the same folder as this program”. The file’s hash equals the hash of the text "hello", because both are the hash of the same five bytes. A hash does not care where the bytes came from.

    Why binary mode matters. A text file’s line endings can differ between Windows and other systems. In text mode Python hides that difference. The bytes are still different, so the hashes are different. Always hash files in "rb" mode.

    Optional detail: reading in chunks. file.read() loads the whole file into memory. For a very large file, you can read a piece at a time and feed each piece to the hash with update. The answer is the same.

    PYTHON 

    def file_hash_in_chunks(path):
    """The same answer as file_hash, but reads a large file a piece at a time."""
    hasher = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path, "rb") as file:
        chunk = file.read(4096)
        while chunk != b"":
            hasher.update(chunk)
            chunk = file.read(4096)
    return hasher.hexdigest()

    file.read(4096) reads at most 4,096 bytes. b"" is an empty bytes value, which means the end of the file. You do not need this version for the course’s small files.

    Use 1: checking a downloaded file

    Many software publishers print the SHA-256 hash of each file on their download page. After you download the file, you calculate its hash yourself and compare.

    PYTHON 

    published = "2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824"
if file_hash(demo) == published:
    print("The file matches the published hash.")
else:
    print("Warning: the file does NOT match. Do not use it.")

    OUTPUT 

    The file matches the published hash.

    If the hashes match, your copy is the same as the publisher’s, byte for byte. If they differ, the download was damaged or the file was changed. Either way, do not use it.

    The same idea lets you prove that a log file or a piece of evidence has not been altered: record its hash when you collect it, and calculate the hash again later.

    Use 2: storing passwords

    A website must check your password when you log in. It should not keep the password itself. If its database were stolen, every password would be exposed.

    Instead, a well-built system stores a hash of the password. At login, it hashes what you typed and compares the two hashes. Because hashing is one-way, a stolen list of hashes does not hand over the passwords directly.

    Real systems go further than plain SHA-256. They add a random value called a salt to each password before hashing, and they use slow, purpose-built password-hashing functions. That is beyond this course. The idea to keep is: store a hash, never the password.

    Common mistakes

    • Forgetting encode. hashlib.sha256("hello") raises TypeError. Hash bytes, not a string.
    • Forgetting .hexdigest(). Without it you print a hash object, not the 64 characters.
    • Opening a file in text mode to hash it. Use "rb".
    • Extra spaces or a newline. "hello\n" is not "hello". If a hash does not match, check for a stray newline or space. strip() helps when you read an expected hash from a file.
    • Calling hashing “encryption”. Encryption can be reversed with a key. Hashing cannot be reversed at all. This week’s Concepts Bridge compares them.
    • Thinking a hash hides a weak password. Anyone can hash the word password and get the same digest as everyone else. That is one reason common passwords are dangerous.
    Challenge

    Exercises: Level 1

    1. Print the SHA-256 hash of your first name in lower case. Check that it has 64 characters.
    2. Print the hash of "Olivia" and of "olivia". Are they the same? Write one sentence in a comment saying why.
    3. Write same_text(a, b). It returns True if the two strings have the same SHA-256 hash. Test it with two equal strings and two that differ by one space.
    4. Use file_hash on the course file assets/files/sample_text.txt. Use this path, which is ready-made: Path(__file__).resolve().parents[4] / "assets" / "files" / "sample_text.txt" (it works from a program in a folder such as lessons/3.2_code/; adjust the number if your program is somewhere else). Print the hash.
    5. Copy sample_text.txt to your own folder. Change one letter in the copy and save it. Hash both files. What do you see? Write one sentence in a comment.
    Challenge

    Exercises: Level 2

    1. Write verify_text(text, expected). It returns True if the hash of text equals expected, ignoring upper and lower case in expected and any spaces around it.
    2. Hash every line of assets/files/common_passwords.txt and print the first three as password -> hash. Remember to strip() each line. This shows why a common password is not protected by hashing alone: its hash is the same everywhere.

    3.3 The Caesar cipher

    The code for this section is in 3.3_code/caesar.py.

    Why look at an old cipher?

    People have hidden messages for thousands of years. The Caesar cipher is named after Julius Caesar, who is said to have used it. It is far too weak for real use today. It is still a good way to practise ord, chr, the % operator and loops over text, and it shows what a cipher is.

    This is a teaching cipher. It is NOT secure. Never use it to protect real data. Section 3.3 ends by explaining why.

    Key terms

    • Plaintext: the message before it is scrambled.
    • Cipher: a method for scrambling text so that only people who know the method and the key can read it.
    • Key: the secret value that controls the scrambling. In the Caesar cipher the key is a number.
    • Encrypt: turn plaintext into scrambled text, called ciphertext.
    • Decrypt: turn ciphertext back into plaintext.

    The idea: shift each letter

    The Caesar cipher moves every letter a fixed number of places along the alphabet. The number is the key. With a key of 3:

    OUTPUT 

    plain:   a b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z
cipher:  d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z a b c

    So a becomes d, b becomes e, and x wraps around to a. The word cat becomes fdw.

    Letters as positions

    In Week 1 you used ord to get a character’s number and chr to turn a number back into a character. For the letters a to z, the numbers run in order, so subtracting ord("a") gives the letter’s position in the alphabet, counting from 0.

    PYTHON 

    print(ord("a"), ord("d"), ord("z"))
print(ord("d") - ord("a"))

    OUTPUT 

    97 100 122
3

    So a is position 0, d is position 3 and z is position 25. Upper-case letters work the same way, starting from ord("A"), which is 65.

    Wrapping around with % 26

    If you add 3 to the position of y (24), you get 27. There is no position 27, because the alphabet has 26 letters. We want to wrap around to the start.

    The remainder operator % gives what is left after dividing. 27 % 26 is 1, so y moves to position 1, which is b.

    PYTHON 

    print((24 + 3) % 26)
print(-3 % 26)

    OUTPUT 

    1
23

    The second line is useful. In Python, % with a positive divisor never gives a negative answer. A shift of -3 from position 0 lands on position 23, which is x. That is why shifting backwards works with no extra code.

    Building shift_letter

    The function must:

    1. Work out whether the character is lower case, upper case, or not a letter.
    2. Leave non-letters (spaces, digits, punctuation) alone.
    3. Convert the letter to a position, add the key, wrap with % 26, and convert back.
    4. Keep the case.

    PYTHON 

    def shift_letter(letter, key):
    """Shift one letter `key` places along the alphabet, keeping its case.

    Anything that is not a letter from a to z or A to Z is returned unchanged.
    """
    if "a" <= letter <= "z":
        start = ord("a")
    elif "A" <= letter <= "Z":
        start = ord("A")
    else:
        return letter
    position = ord(letter) - start
    new_position = (position + key) % 26
    return chr(start + new_position)

    "a" <= letter <= "z" compares characters by their numbers, so it is True for the 26 lower-case letters only. The start variable holds the number where that case begins. Test it:

    PYTHON 

    print(shift_letter("a", 3))
print(shift_letter("y", 3))
print(shift_letter("Y", 3))
print(shift_letter("!", 3))
print(shift_letter("d", -3))

    OUTPUT 

    d
b
B
!
a

    Encrypting a message

    Apply shift_letter to every character, then join the pieces back into one string with "".join(...). (You used join in Week 1.)

    PYTHON 

    def encrypt(text, key):
    """Shift every letter in the text by `key` places."""
    return "".join(shift_letter(ch, key) for ch in text)


secret = encrypt("Meet at the cafe, 9 pm!", 3)
print(secret)

    OUTPUT 

    Phhw dw wkh fdih, 9 sp!

    Case, spaces, the digit and the punctuation are all kept. Only the letters moved.

    Decrypting

    To undo a shift of 3, shift by -3. So decrypting is encrypting with the negative key.

    PYTHON 

    def decrypt(text, key):
    """Undo encrypt by shifting every letter back by `key` places."""
    return encrypt(text, -key)


print(decrypt(secret, 3))

    OUTPUT 

    Meet at the cafe, 9 pm!

    Two more things to try. A key of 13 applied twice gives back the original, because 13 + 13 = 26. A key of 26 changes nothing, because it is a full lap.

    PYTHON 

    print(encrypt("Hello, World!", 13))
print(encrypt("xyz", 26))

    OUTPUT 

    Uryyb, Jbeyq!
xyz

    Letters with accents, such as the é in café, are not in a to z. This version leaves them unchanged. encrypt("café", 1) gives dbgé, with the é left as it was.

    Why this cipher is not secure

    There are only 25 useful keys (1 to 25). Anyone who sees a Caesar ciphertext can try all 25 and read the one that makes sense. That takes a computer a fraction of a second, and a patient person a few minutes. Keeping the method secret does not help, because the method is public knowledge.

    Modern encryption uses standard, carefully tested methods with keys so large that trying them all is impossible. If you ever need to protect real data, use those tools. Do not invent your own cipher, and never use this one.

    This week’s Concepts Bridge compares encryption with hashing and encoding.

    Common mistakes

    • Forgetting the wrap. Without % 26, shifting z gives a character such as {.
    • Forgetting to subtract the start. Using ord(letter) + key directly mixes up positions and character numbers.
    • Treating upper and lower case the same. If you use ord("a") for a capital letter, you get the wrong answer. Choose start for each case.
    • Shifting spaces and punctuation. Return non-letters unchanged.
    • Believing a cipher means security. A weak cipher gives a false sense of safety, which is worse than none.
    Challenge

    Exercises: Level 1

    1. Without running it, work out shift_letter("m", 5), shift_letter("x", 5) and shift_letter("B", 2). Then run them.
    2. Encrypt "Perth is warm" with a key of 4. Then decrypt the result and check you get the original.
    3. Write is_letter(ch). It returns True for a to z and A to Z. Use it to count the letters in "Meet at 9 pm!".
    4. Encrypt the sentence "Keep this a secret" with key 7 and print it. Ask yourself: would you trust this to hide a real password? Write a one-sentence answer in a comment.
    5. Check that decrypt(encrypt(text, key), key) == text for three different texts and keys, including one with capital letters and digits.
    Challenge

    Exercises: Level 2

    1. Write rotate_word(word, key) that shifts only the lower-case letters and leaves capitals alone. Test it.
    2. Change encrypt so it also accepts keys larger than 26 or smaller than -26. Does your program already handle them? Explain why in a comment.

    Concepts Bridge: Hashing, Encryption and Encoding

    Time: 30 minutes. Reading 12 minutes, activities 13 minutes, checking the model answers 5 minutes.

    Why this matters

    People often mix up three ideas: encoding, encryption and hashing. All three change data into a different form, so they look alike. They have different jobs. If you pick the wrong one, you can give a false sense of safety. Choosing the right tool for a job is part of LO 4.

    The three ideas

    • Encoding changes data into another format so that it can be stored or sent. Everyone knows the rules, so anyone can reverse it. UTF-8 (Week 1) is an encoding. So is Base64, which writes bytes using only letters, digits and a few symbols so that they can travel in text.
    • Encryption scrambles data so that only someone with the right key can read it. It is for secrecy. The Caesar cipher (Section 3.3) is a very weak form of encryption.
    • Hashing calculates a short, fixed-length fingerprint of data. It is one-way. It is for integrity and for checking that two things match. SHA-256 (Section 3.2) is a hash.
    Encoding Encryption Hashing
    Purpose Represent data in a usable format Keep data secret Fingerprint data to check it has not changed, or to check a match
    Can it be reversed? Yes, by anyone, because the rules are public Yes, but only by someone with the right key No. It is one-way, for everyone
    Needs a key? No Yes No
    Output length Grows with the input About the same as the input Always the same (64 hex characters for SHA-256)
    Example in this course UTF-8 encode and decode; Base64-style encoding Caesar cipher (weak, for teaching only) hashlib.sha256
    Safe for secrecy? No Yes, if the method is strong and the key stays secret No. It hides nothing about guessable inputs

    The common mix-up: encoding is not security

    Base64 and similar encodings look scrambled. For example, the text hello in Base64 is aGVsbG8=. It is not secret. Anyone can decode it in one line, with no key. If you see a “password” that is only encoded, treat it as if it were written in plain text.

    A second mix-up: “hashing a password encrypts it”. It does not. Nothing can be decrypted, because there is no key and no way back. That is exactly why a website can check a password without being able to read it.

    Choosing the tool

    Ask three questions about the job:

    1. Do I need to get the data back later? If no, hashing may fit. If yes, you need encoding or encryption.
    2. Must the data stay secret from other people? If yes, you need encryption (a strong, standard method, not the Caesar cipher).
    3. Do I only need to know whether the data changed, or whether two values match? That is hashing.
    Challenge

    Activity 1: choose the tool (8 minutes)

    For each scenario, write encoding, encryption or hashing, with a reason in one sentence.

    1. A program saves the text Zoë so that it uses the right bytes in a file.
    2. You want to check that a file you downloaded is the same as the one the publisher posted.
    3. A staff member sends a private message that only the person who receives it should be able to read.
    4. A login system must check a password without keeping the password.
    5. A file stores each byte as letters and digits so that it can be pasted into an email.

    Activity 2: why can’t a site email you your old password? (5 minutes)

    You press “I forgot my password” on a website. It sends a link to choose a new one. Another site emails you your old password. In two or three sentences, explain what the second site’s behaviour tells you about how it stores passwords, and why that is a problem.

    Activity 1

    1. Encoding. The program is only choosing how to represent the characters as bytes (UTF-8). Nothing is hidden.
    2. Hashing. You compare the SHA-256 hash of your copy with the hash the publisher posted. If one byte differs, the hashes differ.
    3. Encryption. The message must stay secret, and only the holder of the key should be able to read it.
    4. Hashing. The system keeps a hash of the password. At login it hashes what you typed and compares the two hashes.
    5. Encoding. Writing bytes as text, such as Base64, is representation. It is not secret, and anyone can undo it.

    Activity 2. If a site can email your old password, it has the password itself, or it stores it in a way it can reverse. A hash cannot be reversed, so a site that stores only a hash cannot tell you the old password. The second site is storing passwords unsafely. If someone stole its database, they would get every password. It is also a risk because email is not private: the password then sits in an inbox. A well-built site stores a hash and lets you set a new password instead.

    Further reading

    • Python Software Foundation (2026) hashlib — Secure hashes and message digests. Available at: https://docs.python.org/3/library/hashlib.html (Accessed: 11 November 2026).
    • Python Software Foundation (2026) base64 — Base16, Base32, Base64, Base85 Data Encodings. Available at: https://docs.python.org/3/library/base64.html (Accessed: 11 November 2026).

    Practice task: Password Strength Checker

    Callout

    Files for this task

    The easiest way to get every file is the course zip file from the Setup page. Unzip it and open the folder in PyCharm. The programs find the data files by their place in that folder, so keep the folder layout. You can also download single files here:

    • starter.py
    • solution.py
    • test_solution.py

    Time: 2 hours. This is your portfolio item for Week 3. Your tutor marks it at the end of the week.

    Goal

    Build a program that rates a password as "weak", "fair" or "strong" and tells the user what is wrong with it, in plain English. You write small functions that take values and return values (pure functions), so they are easy to test. input() and print() stay in main().

    There is also an optional stretch: an integrity checker that hashes a file.

    Privacy and safety notes (read first)

    • Test only with made-up passwords. Never type a real password into a practice program.
    • The program must never save a password, and never print one to a file. It only reads a password, rates it and forgets it.
    • A checker like this can only apply rules. It cannot know whether a password is safe. See your note below.
    • Length matters most. A passphrase (several unrelated words, such as purple teapot morning walk) is long and easy to remember, so it is a good pattern.

    Files

    File What it is
    starter.py The function names and docstrings, with TODO bodies for you to fill in.
    test_solution.py Tests for the functions.
    solution.py A model answer. Try the task yourself before you look.

    The list of common passwords is assets/files/common_passwords.txt (50 common passwords, one per line, in lower case). starter.py already finds it for you with COMMON_FILE.

    The fixed wording

    The tests check these exact messages. starter.py already has them as constants (TOO_SHORT and so on), so use the names.

    Constant Message
    TOO_SHORT It is shorter than 12 characters.
    NO_UPPER It has no upper-case letter.
    NO_LOWER It has no lower-case letter.
    NO_DIGIT It has no digit.
    NO_SYMBOL It has no symbol.
    IS_COMMON It is on the list of common passwords.

    find_problems returns the messages in the order above. An empty list means no problems.

    The rating rule

    strength(password, common) checks these in order:

    1. weak if the password is a common password (ignoring case), or is shorter than 8 characters.
    2. strong if find_problems returns an empty list (no problems at all).
    3. fair for everything else.

    A symbol is any character that is not a letter, a digit or a space.

    Steps (120 minutes)

    Run the tests after each step to see more of them pass. In PyCharm, right-click test_solution.py and choose Run pytest. To test your own file, open test_solution.py and change import solution as checker to import starter as checker. Change it back if you want to compare with the model answer.

    Step What you do Time
    1 Read starter.py from top to bottom. Run it. It should print nothing and not crash. Read the fixed wording and the rating rule above. 10 min
    2 Write load_common_passwords(path). Open the file with with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as file:. For each line, strip() and lower() it, skip empty lines, and add it to a set. Return the set. 10 min
    3 Write check_length, has_upper, has_lower, has_digit and has_symbol. Use any(...) for the four has_ functions. 15 min
    4 Write is_common(password, common). Make the password lower case and test it with in. 5 min
    5 Write find_problems(password, common). Start with an empty list, use a separate if for each check (not elif), and append the matching message. Return the list. 15 min
    6 Write strength(password, common) using the three rules, in order. 10 min
    7 Write main(). Load the list, remind the user to use made-up passwords, then ask for passwords until an empty line. For each one, print the rating and each problem on its own line. 15 min
    8 Run all the tests. Fix anything that fails. Read each failure message carefully, because it shows what the test expected. 15 min
    9 Try your program by hand with five made-up passwords, such as qwerty, Tuesday1, purple teapot morning walk and Blue-Kettle-47-Rain. Check the ratings make sense. 5 min
    10 Write password_note.txt (see below). 15 min
    11 Tidy up: remove unused code and debug print lines, check your docstrings, and make sure no password is saved anywhere. 5 min
    Total 120 min

    Stretch (optional): an integrity checker

    If you have time left inside the 2 hours, or as an optional extra. About 20 minutes. You do not need it to meet the checklist.

    1. Write file_hash(path). Open the file in "rb" mode, read it, and return the SHA-256 hex digest.
    2. Write verify_file(path, expected_hash). Return True if the file’s hash equals expected_hash, ignoring upper and lower case and spaces around expected_hash.

    The last three tests in test_solution.py are for the stretch. They fail until you write these two functions, and that is fine.

    Example run

    OUTPUT 

    Password strength checker.
Use made-up passwords only. Never type a real password here.
Press Enter on an empty line to finish.
Password to check: sunshine
  Rating: weak
  - It is shorter than 12 characters.
  - It has no upper-case letter.
  - It has no digit.
  - It has no symbol.
  - It is on the list of common passwords.
Password to check: purple teapot morning walk
  Rating: fair
  - It has no upper-case letter.
  - It has no digit.
  - It has no symbol.
Password to check: Blue-Kettle-47-Rain
  Rating: strong
  No problems found.
Password to check:
Goodbye.

    Your wording for the lines in main() can differ. The problem messages must match the table above.

    Hints

    • A string method such as isupper() works on one character. To ask about a whole password, use any(ch.isupper() for ch in password).
    • line.strip() removes the newline and spaces at the ends. .lower() makes it lower case.
    • A set is made with set() and filled with .add(item).
    • problems.append(TOO_SHORT) adds one message to a list.
    • Compare lists with ==. An empty list is [].
    • purple teapot morning walk is only “fair” because this checker asks for a capital, a digit and a symbol. That shows a limit of rule-based checkers. Say so in your note.

    Your note: password_note.txt

    Write five or six sentences, in your own words, in a plain text file called password_note.txt. Cover these points:

    1. What does your checker test, and what can it not know?
    2. Why does a list of common passwords matter?
    3. Why does length help?
    4. Why should a website store a hash of a password, and not the password?
    5. What is one limit of rule-based checkers?

    Check your work

    Key Points
    • Each week has four blocks: Watch, Read & practise, Concepts Bridge and Build.
    • Validation means checking data before you use it.
    • An allow-list (what is allowed) is safer than a block-list (what is banned).
    • Report every problem at once so the user can fix them together.
    • A hash is a fixed-length fingerprint of data.
    • The same input always gives the same hash; a tiny change gives a very different one.
    • You cannot work back from a hash to the data.
    • The Caesar cipher shifts every letter by a fixed number.
    • It is a teaching cipher. It is not secure and must never protect real data.
    • Encoding represents data. It is not security.
    • Encryption hides data and can be reversed with the key.
    • Hashing gives a fingerprint and cannot be reversed.
    • Never type or save a real password in a practice program.

    4.1 pip and virtual environments

    Why this matters

    So far, every module you imported came with Python: math, random, csv, json, hashlib. Most data and security work also uses tools that other people wrote and shared. A data analyst uses them to work on a million rows at once. A security analyst uses them to summarise a log and draw a chart for a report.

    These tools do not come with Python. You have to install them. This section shows you how to do that safely and tidily, so you always know what is installed and where.

    The standard library and third-party packages

    The standard library is the set of modules that is installed together with Python. You can import any of them straight away.

    PYTHON 

    import math

print(math.sqrt(49))

    OUTPUT 

    7.0

    A package is a bundle of Python code that somebody has prepared so that other people can install it. A third-party package is a package that is not part of the standard library. “Third-party” just means it was written by someone other than you or the Python team. NumPy is a third-party package.

    If you try to import a third-party package that is not installed, Python stops with an error:

    PYTHON 

    import numpy

    OUTPUT 

    ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy'

    This error does not mean your code is wrong. It means the package is not installed in the place Python is looking.

    Most third-party packages are published on PyPI, the Python Package Index (https://pypi.org). PyPI is a public website that stores packages so that anyone can download them. The tool that downloads a package from PyPI and installs it is called pip. pip comes with Python, so you already have it.

    Standard library Third-party package
    Examples math, csv, json, hashlib numpy, pandas, matplotlib
    Comes with Python? Yes No
    Needs pip install? No Yes
    Where it comes from The Python team Other people and organisations, usually through PyPI

    What a virtual environment is

    A virtual environment is a private folder of packages that belongs to one project. When you install a package into it, only that project can see the package.

    Why not install everything in one shared place? There are two reasons.

    1. Projects do not clash. Suppose an old project needs an old version of a package, and a new project needs the newest version. With one shared place, you can only have one version, so one project breaks. With a virtual environment each, both projects keep working.
    2. You know exactly what is installed. The folder holds only what this project needs. You can list it, and you can give that list to another person so their copy of the project works the same way as yours.

    Think of it like a toolbox for each job. The plumber’s toolbox and the electrician’s toolbox hold different tools, and nobody has to dig through one giant pile.

    Finding your virtual environment in PyCharm

    When you create a new project, PyCharm offers to create a virtual environment for it. By default it is a folder called .venv inside the project folder. You do not need to open this folder or edit anything in it. PyCharm and pip look after it.

    To see which environment your project uses:

    1. Open Settings. On Windows and Linux this is File > Settings. On macOS it is PyCharm > Settings.
    2. Choose Project: (your project name) > Python Interpreter.
    3. Look at the top of the page. The interpreter is the Python program that runs your code. Its path should end with .venv and the name of your project should be in it. Below it is a table of the packages installed in this environment.

    📷 Image placeholder: episodes/fig/python_interpreter_settings.png — the Settings window open at Project > Python Interpreter, showing the .venv interpreter path and the table of installed packages.

    If the interpreter line says No interpreter, click Add Interpreter > Add Local Interpreter, choose Virtualenv Environment and New, and click OK. PyCharm then creates the .venv folder for you. The exact wording of these buttons changes a little between PyCharm versions.

    PyCharm also has a Python Packages tool window. Open it with View > Tool Windows > Python Packages. It lists the installed packages and lets you search PyPI for new ones.

    📷 Image placeholder: episodes/fig/python_packages_tool_window.png — the Python Packages tool window at the bottom of PyCharm, with numpy typed in the search box and the installed packages listed.

    Installing NumPy with pip

    You will install packages by typing a command, because the same command works on every computer.

    1. Open the Terminal tool window in PyCharm. It is at the bottom of the window, or under View > Tool Windows > Terminal. The terminal is a place to type commands for the computer, not Python code.
    2. Look at the start of the line where you type. It should begin with (.venv). That tells you the terminal is using the virtual environment of your project.
    3. Type this command and press Enter:

    OUTPUT 

    python -m pip install numpy

    📷 Image placeholder: episodes/fig/terminal_pip_install.png — the PyCharm Terminal showing the (.venv) prompt and the command python -m pip install numpy with its “Successfully installed” line.

    The command has four parts:

    Part Meaning
    python Run the Python that belongs to this environment.
    -m pip Run the module called pip.
    install The job you want pip to do.
    numpy The name of the package on PyPI.

    Writing python -m pip instead of just pip makes sure that the package goes into the same Python that runs your code.

    pip prints a few lines while it downloads. The last line looks something like this. Your version number may be different.

    OUTPUT 

    Successfully installed numpy-2.5.4

    Now test it. Create a new Python file, type these lines and run it:

    PYTHON 

    import numpy

print("NumPy version:", numpy.__version__)

    OUTPUT 

    NumPy version: 2.5.4

    If you see a version number, NumPy is ready. The file 4.1_code/check_numpy.py does the same check with a little more detail.

    You install NumPy once for each project, not each time you run a program. This week you install numpy. You will install pandas in Week 5 and matplotlib in Week 6 in exactly the same way.

    Checking what is installed

    Two more pip commands are useful. Type them in the Terminal.

    pip list shows every package in the environment, with its version:

    OUTPUT 

    python -m pip list

    OUTPUT 

    Package Version
------- -------
numpy   2.5.4
pip     25.3

    Your list and your version numbers will differ. You may also see a few packages that you did not ask for. Some packages need other packages to work, and pip installs those for you.

    pip show gives details about one package:

    OUTPUT 

    python -m pip show numpy

    OUTPUT 

    Name: numpy
Version: 2.5.4
Summary: Fundamental package for array computing in Python
Home-page: https://numpy.org

    There are more lines than this. The useful ones are the name, the version, the summary and where the package is stored.

    The requirements file

    A requirements file is a plain text file, usually called requirements.txt, that lists the packages a project needs, one name on each line. Another person can then install everything in one step with python -m pip install -r requirements.txt. You do not have to write one this week, but you will see this file in many projects, and now you know what it is for.

    A safety habit

    A package is code that runs on your computer, so install only well-known packages that your course, your workplace or a trusted source tells you to use. Check the spelling of the name before you press Enter, because a wrong name can install a different package from the one you meant.

    Common mistakes

    • Typing the command in the wrong place. python -m pip install numpy goes in the Terminal. It is not Python code. If you type it in a .py file you get a SyntaxError.
    • Installing into a different environment. If the Terminal line does not start with (.venv), or the interpreter in Settings is not the one for this project, the package goes somewhere else and import numpy still fails. Check the interpreter in Settings first.
    • Naming your own file numpy.py. Python then imports your file instead of the real package, and you get strange errors. Never give a file the same name as a module you import. The same goes for csv.py, random.py and json.py.
    • Installing again and again. One install per project is enough. If pip says Requirement already satisfied, the package is already there.
    • Mixing up the two names. Sometimes the name you install is not the name you import. For the three packages in this course they are the same: numpy, pandas and matplotlib.
    Challenge

    Exercises: Level 1

    Budget about 3 minutes for each exercise.

    1. Open Settings > Project > Python Interpreter in your PyCharm project. Write down the path of the interpreter. Does it contain .venv?
    2. In the PyCharm Terminal, run python -m pip install numpy. Then run python -m pip list. Write down the version of NumPy you have.
    3. Run python -m pip show numpy. Find the Summary line and the Location line. In one sentence, say what the Location line tells you.
    4. Sort these modules into two groups, “standard library” and “third-party”: json, numpy, hashlib, pandas, csv, matplotlib, math.
    5. In two sentences of your own, explain to a workmate why each project has its own virtual environment.
    Challenge

    Exercises: Level 2

    Optional.

    1. Create a file called requirements.txt in your project with one line, numpy. Run python -m pip install -r requirements.txt in the Terminal. Read what pip prints, and explain why it did not download anything.
    2. Open the Python Packages tool window and search for pandas. Read the description that PyCharm shows. Do not install it yet. Which organisation or project publishes it?
    3. Run python -m pip --version in the Terminal. The line it prints includes a folder path. What does that path tell you about which environment pip belongs to?

    4.2 NumPy arrays

    Why this matters

    A security analyst might have a count of logins for every user on every day of a month. A data analyst might have thousands of prices. In both cases you want to ask questions such as “which counts are above 5?” or “what is every value in dollars instead of cents?”

    With a plain list you write a loop for each question. NumPy lets you ask the question about the whole collection in one line. This section shows you how. Make sure you installed NumPy in Section 4.1 first.

    Importing NumPy and making an array

    NumPy is nearly always imported with a short nickname, np. Everybody who uses NumPy does this, so you will see it in every example you read.

    PYTHON 

    import numpy as np

    as np means “call it np in this file”. An array is NumPy’s collection of numbers. You make one from a list with np.array.

    PYTHON 

    logins = np.array([4, 5, 5, 4, 9, 3, 12])
print(logins)
print(type(logins))

    OUTPUT 

    [ 4  5  5  4  9  3 12]
<class 'numpy.ndarray'>

    Notice that the array prints without commas. The type is numpy.ndarray. The name stands for “n-dimensional array”.

    All the examples in this section are in 4.2_code/arrays_1d.py and 4.2_code/arrays_2d.py. Type them out and run them.

    Shape, ndim and dtype

    Every array has three facts you can look up.

    PYTHON 

    print("shape:", logins.shape)
print("ndim:", logins.ndim)
print("dtype:", logins.dtype)

    OUTPUT 

    shape: (7,)
ndim: 1
dtype: int64
    • shape is a tuple that gives the size in each direction. (7,) means one direction with 7 items.
    • ndim is the number of directions (dimensions). A flat row of numbers has 1. A table has 2.
    • dtype is the data type of the items. int64 means whole numbers stored in 64 bits. An array holds only one dtype. If you mix whole numbers and decimals, NumPy turns every item into a decimal (float64). The exact dtype on your computer may be different, for example int32 on some systems. That is fine.

    Arithmetic on a whole array

    Here is the idea that makes NumPy useful. Arithmetic works on every item at once.

    PYTHON 

    print(logins * 2)
print(logins + 10)
print(logins / 2)

    OUTPUT 

    [ 8 10 10  8 18  6 24]
[14 15 15 14 19 13 22]
[2.  2.5 2.5 2.  4.5 1.5 6. ]

    Working on a whole array in one step is called vectorised arithmetic. The word comes from “vector”, another name for a one-dimensional list of numbers. You do not write the loop. NumPy does it for you.

    You can also combine two arrays of the same shape. The items are paired up by position.

    PYTHON 

    weekend_extra = np.array([0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 2])
print(logins + weekend_extra)

    OUTPUT 

    [ 4  5  5  4  9  5 14]

    Compare this with lists. [1, 2, 3] + [10, 20, 30] joins two lists into one list of six items. np.array([1, 2, 3]) + np.array([10, 20, 30]) adds item by item and gives [11 22 33]. The same symbol does two different jobs, so always check which type you have.

    Indexing and slicing in one dimension

    Indexing and slicing work just like lists.

    PYTHON 

    print(logins[0])
print(logins[-1])
print(logins[1:4])

    OUTPUT 

    4
12
[5 5 4]

    logins[1:4] gives the items at positions 1, 2 and 3. The stop position (4) is not included, as with lists.

    Two-dimensional arrays

    A table of numbers is a two-dimensional array. You make it from a list of lists. Each inner list is one row. A column is made of the item at the same position in every row.

    PYTHON 

    table = np.array([
    [4, 8, 1, 6],
    [5, 5, 3, 9],
    [5, 5, 2, 7],
])
print(table)
print("shape:", table.shape)

    OUTPUT 

    [[4 8 1 6]
 [5 5 3 9]
 [5 5 2 7]]
shape: (3, 4)

    The shape (3, 4) means 3 rows and 4 columns. Here the rows are days and the columns are users.

    To pick one cell, give the row and then the column, separated by a comma: table[row, col]. Counting starts at 0.

    PYTHON 

    print(table[0, 1])
print(table[2, 3])

    OUTPUT 

    8
7

    To pick a whole row or a whole column, use a slice. A lone colon : means “everything in this direction”.

    PYTHON 

    print(table[1])
print(table[:, 0])
print(table[:, -1])
print(table[0:2, 2:4])

    OUTPUT 

    [5 5 3 9]
[4 5 5]
[6 9 7]
[[1 6]
 [3 9]]

    Read table[:, 0] as “all rows, column 0”. That is the first user’s count for every day. The last line takes rows 0 and 1, and columns 2 and 3.

    Boolean masks

    A comparison on an array gives an array of True and False values, one for each item. This is called a boolean mask.

    PYTHON 

    busy = logins > 5
print(busy)

    OUTPUT 

    [False False False False  True False  True]

    Use the mask inside square brackets to keep only the items where it is True.

    PYTHON 

    print(logins[busy])
print(logins[logins > 5])
print("Busy days:", busy.sum())

    OUTPUT 

    [ 9 12]
[ 9 12]
Busy days: 2

    The second line is the usual way to write it. The third line shows a handy trick: True counts as 1 and False as 0, so .sum() on a mask counts how many items matched. Masks also work on tables, and the result is a flat array of the matching items.

    PYTHON 

    print(table > 5)
print(table[table > 5])

    OUTPUT 

    [[False  True False  True]
 [False False False  True]
 [False False False  True]]
[8 6 9 7]

    You can put in >=, <, == and != as well.

    Making arrays with arange and zeros

    You do not always want to type every value.

    PYTHON 

    print(np.arange(5))
print(np.arange(2, 11, 2))
print(np.zeros(4))
print(np.zeros(4, dtype=int))

    OUTPUT 

    [0 1 2 3 4]
[ 2  4  6  8 10]
[0. 0. 0. 0.]
[0 0 0 0]
    • np.arange works like range. np.arange(2, 11, 2) starts at 2, stops before 11 and steps by 2. The result is an array.
    • np.zeros makes an array full of zeros. By default these are decimals (0.). Add dtype=int for whole numbers.
    • For a table, give the shape as a tuple: np.zeros((2, 3), dtype=int) makes 2 rows and 3 columns of zeros. You can then fill in a cell with blank[0, 1] = 7.

    Common mistakes

    • Forgetting import numpy as np. You get NameError: name 'np' is not defined.
    • Using table[0][1] and table[0, 1] as if they were different. Both work on arrays, but table[0, 1] is the NumPy style and it is the one you should use. Slicing like table[:, 0] only works with the comma style.
    • Adding arrays of different shapes. np.array([1, 2, 3]) + np.array([1, 2]) fails with a ValueError that says the shapes could not be broadcast together. The two arrays must have matching shapes.
    • Expecting an array to hold mixed types. np.array([1, "a"]) turns the number into text. Keep an array to numbers only.
    Challenge

    Exercises: Level 1

    Budget about 3 minutes for each exercise. Use this array in tasks 1 to 3: times = np.array([20, 22, 19, 21, 95, 23]) (response times in milliseconds).

    1. Print the shape, ndim and dtype of times. Say what each one tells you.
    2. Print times in seconds (divide by 1000). Does the original times change?
    3. Make a mask for times above 50. Print the mask, then print the matching times, then print how many there are.
    4. Make this table, with days as rows and users as columns: [[3, 7, 2], [4, 6, 9], [5, 5, 1]]. Print the cell for the second day and third user. Print the whole second column.
    5. Use np.arange to make the array [0, 5, 10, 15, 20]. Then use np.zeros to make a table of zeros with 3 rows and 2 columns, made of whole numbers.
    Challenge

    Exercises: Level 2

    Optional.

    1. Using the table from task 4, print only the values that are 5 or more.
    2. Multiply the table from task 4 by np.array([1, 2, 3]). Print the result and describe in a sentence what NumPy did. (This is called broadcasting. You do not need to know the word yet.)
    3. Make np.arange(1, 13) and look up the reshape method in the NumPy documentation. Turn it into a table of 3 rows and 4 columns.

    4.3 Statistics with NumPy

    Why this matters

    Suppose one account downloads far more data than usual, or one user logs in far more often than usual. How do you decide what “far more” means? You compare the value with that account’s normal pattern. Statistics gives you simple numbers for the normal pattern, and a way to measure how far a value is from it.

    This section uses NumPy to work out those numbers. The Build this week uses them to look for unusual login counts. Code for this section is in 4.3_code/statistics_basics.py and 4.3_code/z_scores.py.

    Sum, mean, median, min, max and argmax

    Here are response times in milliseconds for eight requests to a web page. One of them is very slow.

    PYTHON 

    import numpy as np

times = np.array([20, 22, 19, 21, 20, 23, 95, 20])

print("sum:   ", times.sum())
print("mean:  ", times.mean())
print("median:", np.median(times))
print("min:   ", times.min())
print("max:   ", times.max())
print("argmax:", times.argmax())

    OUTPUT 

    sum:    240
mean:   30.0
median: 20.5
min:    19
max:    95
argmax: 6
    • The mean is the total divided by the count. It is the usual meaning of “average”.
    • The median is the middle value when the numbers are sorted. With an even count, it is halfway between the two middle values. Here those are 20 and 21.
    • argmax gives the position of the biggest value, not the value itself. The 95 is at position 6. There is also argmin for the smallest.

    Notice that the one slow request pulls the mean up to 30, while the median stays near 20. When a few values are extreme, the median often describes a typical value better. Most functions can be written two ways: times.mean() or np.mean(times). Both do the same thing. median is only written as np.median(times).

    Standard deviation

    The standard deviation is a measure of spread. It tells you how far values typically sit from the mean. A small standard deviation means the values are close together. A large one means they are spread out.

    This course uses the population standard deviation, which is what np.std gives by default. Here is how to work it out by hand for the values 2, 4, 4 and 6.

    1. Find the mean: (2 + 4 + 4 + 6) / 4 = 4.
    2. Subtract the mean from each value: -2, 0, 0, 2.
    3. Square each difference: 4, 0, 0, 4. (Squaring makes every number positive.)
    4. Find the mean of those squares: (4 + 0 + 0 + 4) / 4 = 2.
    5. Take the square root: the square root of 2 is about 1.41.

    NumPy does all five steps for you:

    PYTHON 

    values = np.array([2, 4, 4, 6])
print("np.std:", values.std())

    OUTPUT 

    np.std: 1.4142135623730951

    You can follow the steps in NumPy too. 4.3_code/statistics_basics.py does that. Read it and compare it with the steps above.

    Axis: down the columns or along the rows

    On a table, sum, mean, max and the rest can work on the whole table, down each column, or along each row. You choose with axis.

    PYTHON 

    table = np.array([
    [4, 8, 1, 6],
    [5, 5, 3, 9],
    [5, 5, 2, 7],
])
print("whole table:", table.sum())
print("axis=0:", table.sum(axis=0))
print("axis=1:", table.sum(axis=1))

    OUTPUT 

    whole table: 60
axis=0: [14 18  6 22]
axis=1: [19 22 19]
    • axis=0 works down the rows, so you get one answer for each column. With days as rows and users as columns, that is one answer per user.
    • axis=1 works along each row, so you get one answer for each row. That is one answer per day.

    A way to remember it: the axis you name is the one that disappears. A table of shape (3, 4) summed with axis=0 leaves shape (4,). Summed with axis=1 it leaves (3,).

    PYTHON 

    print("mean per user:", table.mean(axis=0))
print("max per day:", table.max(axis=1))
print("busiest day position:", table.sum(axis=1).argmax())

    OUTPUT 

    mean per user: [4.66666667 6.         2.         7.33333333]
max per day: [8 9 7]
busiest day position: 1

    The last line first adds up each day ([19 22 19]), then asks for the position of the biggest total. That is position 1, the second day.

    The z-score

    How far from normal is a value? The z-score answers in a unit that works for any data:

    OUTPUT 

    z = (value - mean) / std

    A z-score is “how many standard deviations the value is from the mean”. A z-score of 0 means exactly the mean. A z-score of 2 means two standard deviations above. A z-score of -2 means two below.

    A common rule of thumb says that a z-score with an absolute value above 3 (written |z| > 3) is unusual. In many data sets, values this far from the mean are rare. This is only a rule of thumb. Some teams use 2 or 2.5.

    Because NumPy is vectorised, one line gives a z-score for every value. Here are the megabytes downloaded by one account on each of ten days.

    PYTHON 

    downloads = np.array([50, 52, 48, 51, 49, 50, 53, 47, 50, 120])

mean = downloads.mean()
std = downloads.std()
z = (downloads - mean) / std
print(f"mean = {mean:.1f}, std = {std:.2f}")
print(np.round(z, 2))

    OUTPUT 

    mean = 57.0, std = 21.07
[-0.33 -0.24 -0.43 -0.28 -0.38 -0.33 -0.19 -0.47 -0.33  2.99]

    Now use a mask to find the values with a large |z|. np.abs gives the absolute value of every item.

    PYTHON 

    mask = np.abs(z) > 2.5
print("Flagged values:", downloads[mask])

    OUTPUT 

    Flagged values: [120]

    A caution about unusual values

    Look again at that example. The 120 has a z-score of 2.99, which is just under 3. The rule of thumb would not flag it, yet it is more than double every other day.

    The reason is that an extreme value pulls the mean and the standard deviation towards itself. The mean rose from 50.0 to 57.0 and the standard deviation grew from 1.76 to 21.07. A bigger standard deviation makes every z-score smaller. With only ten values, one huge value can partly hide itself. The z-score is still useful, but it is a tool, not a verdict.

    Also remember that unusual is not the same as wrong or malicious. A user might log in 41 times in a day because a script ran by mistake, a shared account was used, a system was tested, or because someone really did something suspicious. The z-score cannot tell you which. It is a prompt to look closer. A person should check the logs around that time before drawing a conclusion.

    Common mistakes

    • Mixing up the axes. If you get one answer per user when you wanted one per day, swap axis=0 and axis=1. Check the shape of the result.
    • Forgetting that argmax gives a position. To get the matching date, use that position to index a list of dates.
    • Dividing by a standard deviation of 0. If every value is the same, std is 0 and the z-score is not defined. NumPy gives nan or inf and prints a warning.
    • Trusting 3 as a law. It is a rule of thumb. Small data sets and extreme values can break it.
    • Calling a flagged value an attack. It is a value to investigate.
    Challenge

    Exercises: Level 1

    Budget about 3 minutes for each exercise.

    1. For np.array([3, 8, 1, 9, 6]), print the sum, mean, median and standard deviation. Check the mean by hand.
    2. Using the same array, print argmax() and the value at that position. Then print argmin().
    3. Work out the population standard deviation of [1, 3, 5, 7] by hand, using the five steps. Write each step down. Then check with np.std.
    4. Make table = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]). Print the sum of each column and the sum of each row. Which axis is which?
    5. Make np.array([10, 20, 30, 40]). Work out the z-score of every value, using vectorised arithmetic. Print them rounded to 2 places. Why is the middle pair symmetrical, one negative and one positive?
    6. Make np.array([12, 15, 11, 40, 13]). Find the values with |z| above 1.5. Then add a sentence of your own about what you would do next with a flagged value.
    Challenge

    Exercises: Level 2

    Optional.

    1. Take the array in task 6 and remove the 40. How do the mean and standard deviation change?
    2. Make a table of 5 rows and 3 columns of your own numbers. Print the z-scores of each column, using axis=0 to get the means and standard deviations.
    3. Read the NumPy documentation for np.std and find out what the ddof argument does. This course does not use it.

    Concepts Bridge: Why Arrays Are Faster than Lists

    Time: 30 minutes. Reading 12 minutes, running the timing code 5 minutes, activities 8 minutes, checking the model answer 5 minutes.

    Why this matters

    LO 4 asks you to judge which tool or method suits a problem. This week you have two tools for a list of numbers: a plain Python list with a loop, and a NumPy array. Neither is always better. A good analyst can say which to use, and why. This bridge explains what is different inside each one, shows a small timing test, and gives you a way to decide.

    What is different inside

    Python list NumPy array
    What it holds References (pointers) to separate objects, which can be any type One block of numbers, all the same type
    Mixed types? Yes: [1, "a", 2.5] No: everything becomes one dtype
    Adding an item Easy and cheap: append Awkward: the size is fixed, so NumPy makes a new array
    Maths on every item You write a for loop One expression, such as a * 2
    Where the loop runs Line by line in Python In compiled code (code already translated to run fast on the machine)

    A list is like a shelf of labelled boxes, where each box can hold anything and the labels point to other places. An array is like one long tray of identical slots. The tray is packed tightly, so the computer can move along it quickly. That is the first reason arrays are fast.

    The second reason is about the loop. When you write for number in numbers:, Python reads and carries out your instructions one line at a time, for every item. When you write np.sum(numbers_array), the loop runs inside NumPy’s compiled code, which does not have the line-by-line cost.

    A small timing test

    The file bridge_code/timing_comparison.py adds up the numbers from 0 to 999,999 in three ways: a for loop, the built-in sum() on a list, and np.sum() on an array. It measures each one with time.perf_counter(). This function gives the current time in seconds, so the difference between the time before and after a job is how long the job took.

    Type it out and run it in PyCharm. Here is typical output. Your numbers will differ, and they will change from one run to the next.

    OUTPUT 

    Totals: 499999500000 499999500000 499999500000
for loop: 0.0677 seconds
sum():    0.0059 seconds
np.sum(): 0.0009 seconds

    All three give the same total. Timing depends on your computer, what else it is doing and the version of Python and NumPy. Do not quote an exact “times faster” number as a fact. What you can say is that on a large set of numbers, the array version is usually much quicker than the plain loop.

    Also notice what the test does not show. Making the array from a list takes time too. If you only add up a handful of numbers, the saving is too small to matter.

    Choosing: list or array?

    Use this table to judge a problem.

    Question A list and a loop is better when… An array is better when…
    How much data? There are a few dozen items There are thousands or millions of items
    What types? The items are mixed (names, numbers, dates) Every item is a number of the same kind
    How does the data grow? You add one item at a time as you go You have all the data first, then calculate
    What is the job? Reading, filtering or building text Maths on whole columns (mean, z-score, totals)
    Who reads the code? A short script where the loop is the clearest thing The array line is as clear as the loop, and shorter

    Speed is only one reason. Clarity matters too. values.mean() says what it does, and there is less room for a mistake than in a hand-written loop. But a loop is still the right tool when you must read a file line by line, when each item needs a decision, or when you are only working with ten numbers.

    Challenge

    Activity 1: choose list or array (5 minutes)

    For each task, say list or array, and give one reason.

    1. Keep a record of the names of users as they sign in during the day, adding each one when it happens.
    2. Calculate the z-score of 500,000 download sizes in megabytes.
    3. Store a short record with a user name, a login time and a number of failed attempts.
    4. Convert 20,000 temperatures from degrees Celsius to degrees Fahrenheit.

    Activity 2: predict the result (3 minutes)

    Do not run this. Work out what it prints, then check in PyCharm.

    PYTHON 

    import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(a * 3 + 1)
print(a[a > 2].sum())

    Activity 1.

    1. List. The data grows one item at a time, and the items are text. An array is awkward to grow.
    2. Array. A very large amount of same-type numbers, and maths on a whole column.
    3. List (or a dictionary or tuple). The items are mixed types: text, a time and a number. An array holds one type.
    4. Array. Large, same-type numbers, and one expression does the job: celsius * 9 / 5 + 32.

    Activity 2.

    OUTPUT 

    [ 4  7 10 13]
7

    a * 3 + 1 works on each item: 1 becomes 4, 2 becomes 7, 3 becomes 10 and 4 becomes 13. The mask a > 2 is [False False True True], so a[a > 2] is [3 4] and the sum is 7.

    Now think about your Build this week. You write the same mean twice, once as a loop (mean_loop) and once with an array (user_means). Your written note compares them using the table above.

    Further reading

    • Harris, C.R. et al. (2020) ‘Array programming with NumPy’, Nature, 585, pp. 357–362. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2649-2 (Accessed: 11 November 2026).
    • NumPy Developers (2026) NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners. Available at: https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/absolute_beginners.html (Accessed: 11 November 2026).
    • Python Software Foundation (2026) time — Time access and conversions. Available at: https://docs.python.org/3/library/time.html (Accessed: 11 November 2026).

    Practice task: Login Statistics with a Z-Score Check

    Callout

    Files for this task

    The easiest way to get every file is the course zip file from the Setup page. Unzip it and open the folder in PyCharm. The programs find the data files by their place in that folder, so keep the folder layout. You can also download single files here:

    • starter.py
    • solution.py
    • test_solution.py

    Time: 2 hours. This is your portfolio item for Week 4. Your tutor marks it at the end of the week.

    Goal

    You have a table of daily login counts: 28 days and 6 users. Your program reads it into a NumPy array, works out each user’s mean and standard deviation, finds the busiest day, and uses z-scores to list counts that are unusual for that user. You also write the mean twice, once with a loop and once with NumPy, so you can judge which tool suits the job (LO 4).

    Before you start

    1. Make sure the project you are working in has its own virtual environment (Section 4.1).
    2. Open the Terminal in PyCharm. The line should start with (.venv).
    3. Install the two packages this task needs:

    OUTPUT 

    python -m pip install numpy pytest
    1. Open assets/data/login_counts.csv and read it. The first row is a header: date,user01,user02,user03,user04,user05,user06. There are 28 rows after it, one for each day starting on 2026-10-05. Each cell is the number of logins that user made that day. All of the data is made up for this course.

    Files

    File What it is
    starter.py Your functions to fill in, with a TODO list in each.
    test_solution.py Tests for the functions.
    solution.py A model answer. Try the task yourself before you look.
    method_note.txt You create this. Your written note (see below).

    starter.py finds the data file with Path(__file__), so it runs from PyCharm whichever folder you start it from, as long as you keep the course folder layout. If you copy the files to another project, change COUNTS_FILE to point at your copy of login_counts.csv.

    Steps

    1. (5 min) Open starter.py and read it. Run it. It should run and print nothing. Near the bottom, leave the two if __name__ == "__main__": lines as they are.
    2. (20 min) Write load_counts(path). Use the csv module from Week 2 (not Pandas). It returns (dates, users, counts). dates is a list of 28 strings, users is a list of 6 names, and counts is a 2-D NumPy array of whole numbers with shape (28, 6). Check it in main() with print(counts.shape).
    3. (10 min) Write mean_loop(values). Use a plain for loop. Do not use sum(), np.mean or .mean().
    4. (15 min) Write user_means(counts), user_stds(counts) and daily_totals(counts). Each is one line. Decide whether you need axis=0 or axis=1.
    5. (10 min) Write busiest_day(dates, counts). It returns the date and the total for the day with the most logins. Use argmax.
    6. (15 min) Write z_scores(counts). One vectorised line gives a 2-D array the same shape as counts. Each cell is compared with the mean and standard deviation of its own column.
    7. (15 min) Write unusual(dates, users, counts, threshold=3.0). It returns a list of (date, user, count, z) tuples where the absolute value of z is above the threshold. Round z to 2 decimal places and sort the list by date.
    8. (15 min) Write main(). Print a table of each user’s mean and standard deviation, the busiest day, and the unusual values. Also print one user’s mean from mean_loop and from user_means, to show that they agree.
    9. (5 min) Run the tests. Fix any that fail.
    10. (10 min) Write your note in method_note.txt. Tidy up your code: remove any test print lines, and check that every function has its docstring.

    Minutes: 5 + 20 + 10 + 15 + 10 + 15 + 15 + 15 + 5 + 10 = 120.

    Example run

    Your wording can differ, but the numbers should match.

    OUTPUT 

    Loaded 28 days for 6 users.

User        Mean   Std dev
user01      4.21      1.01
user02      6.46      2.65
user03      2.89      1.18
user04      9.50      6.16
user05      4.89      1.05
user06      7.43      1.24

Mean for user01 with a loop: 4.21
Mean for user01 with NumPy:  4.21

Busiest day: 2026-10-21 with 71 logins in total.

Unusual values (z-score above 3 or below -3):
  2026-10-21  user04   41 logins  z = 5.11
  2026-10-28  user02   19 logins  z = 4.73
Unusual is not the same as wrong. Each one needs a closer look.

    Hints

    • With the csv module, next(reader) gives you the header row. After that, loop over reader for the data rows. Every cell is text, so use int(cell).
    • np.array(list_of_lists) makes a 2-D array. Each inner list becomes one row.
    • Use axis=0 for “one answer per user” (down each column) and axis=1 for “one answer per day” (along each row).
    • totals.argmax() is a position. Use it to look up the date in the dates list. Wrap a NumPy number in int(...) when you return it.
    • Subtracting a 1-D array of column means from the 2-D array subtracts each user’s mean from that user’s column. That is why z_scores can be a single line.
    • Use z[row, col] for a cell. A nested loop over range(len(dates)) and range(len(users)) visits every cell. Wrap the z value as float(z[row, col]) before you round it.
    • found.sort() sorts a list of tuples by the first item, which is the date. The date text 2026-10-21 sorts correctly because the year comes first.
    • f-string alignment (Week 1): {name:<8} pads on the right and {value:>8.2f} pads on the left with 2 decimal places.
    • Keep print() inside main() only. Functions that take values in and return values are pure and easy to test.

    Your written note: method_note.txt

    Write five or six sentences, in your own words, in a plain text file called method_note.txt. Put it in the same folder as your code. Cover these:

    1. Compare mean_loop with user_means. Which is shorter? Which would you trust more, and why?
    2. When would a loop still be the right tool?
    3. What did the z-score check find in this data?
    4. What should a security analyst do next with a flagged value? Does a high z-score prove an attack?

    Check your work

    Key Points
    • Each week has four blocks: Watch, Read & practise, Concepts Bridge and Build.
    • A virtual environment is a private set of packages for one project.
    • Install with python -m pip install, inside the project.
    • Install only well-known packages and check the spelling of the name.
    • An array holds numbers of one type in one block.
    • Arithmetic on an array works on every item at once (vectorised).
    • A boolean mask such as a[a > 5] picks the items that pass a test.
    • The standard deviation measures how spread out values are.
    • axis=0 works down each column; axis=1 works along each row.
    • A z-score above 3 is unusual. That is a reason to look closer, not proof of a problem.
    • An array holds one type of number in one block, so the loop runs in fast compiled code.
    • For small data, mixed types or a short script, a list and a loop can be clearer.
    • An unusual value is a reason to look closer, not proof of an attack.
